_note: Founder access: a sign-in for the founder alone, and a guarded reveal of the two Azure keys the assistant service holds, in the Control Tower's GilbertOne screens. Every number and every name the feature runs on lives here once — the service (apps/assistant-api/src/lib/founder-access.ts), the provisioning script (deploy/ops/configure-founder-access.sh, which cannot read JSON on the box and is held to these values by scripts/check-boundaries.mjs) and the screen (apps/web/src/lib/founder-access.ts) all read it. The refusal sentences are the routes' own, in packages/catalog/apis/assistant.json. It is dark by default: nothing a deploy does can switch it on, and the four routes refuse until the service's environment carries both the enable line and a credential. docs/governance/FOUNDER-ACCESS.md is the account of what it is and what it is not.

decision.what: A founder login and a guarded eye reveal of the two Azure keys in the Control Tower, built production-grade and dark by default.
decision.amends: docs/PROMPT-CONTROL-TOWER-UI.md §1 ("API keys never reach the browser in full") and §12 ("Do not reveal a full key to the browser") for exactly one caller — the founder, signed in with a password and an authenticator code, typing a fresh code for each reveal — and exactly two keys. Every other administration screen, every other key and every other person is held to §1 and §12 unchanged.
decision.why: The founder holds the Azure resources and is the one person who re-enters a key when one is malformed (docs/governance/ASSISTANT-ACTIVATION.md: the speech key stored on 22 September was 140 characters with spaces in it). Reading the key back without a terminal on the box is what was asked for; the controls below are what make it something other than a key on a web page.
decision.amendment: The founder's instruction of 28 September 2026: sign in once with the password and the authenticator code, for two hours rather than fifteen minutes, and let that one sign-in also unlock changing settings on the Control Tower — the Configuration tab, GilbertOne's Voice and Speech settings — because today the founder is the only person who has access. A reveal of a key still needs a fresh code each time. Where founder access is switched off, or the service does not answer, the settings editors stay a preview held in the tab's memory and say so; the gate is enforced in the browser until the service keeps a settings history and enforces it itself.

enable.why: The switch is its own line, written by hand, exactly as the production acknowledgement is: configure-founder-access.sh writes the credential and never this line, and no deploy writes either file. A credential typed and a feature switched on are two decisions, taken as two acts.

scrypt.why: scrypt from node:crypto, at the parameters OWASP's password storage guidance gives as its floor for scrypt (N = 2^17, r = 8, p = 1): 128 MiB and a noticeable fraction of a second per guess, paid only on a sign-in the lockout has not already refused. The parameters travel inside the stored hash, so a stronger hash written later is read without a code change; the service refuses to treat anything weaker than these as a credential at all. The separator is a colon, not a dollar sign, because the hash lives in a systemd EnvironmentFile and a dollar sign there is a character somebody will one day expect to be expanded.

credential._totpSecretBytesWhy: Twenty random bytes, base32-encoded — RFC 4226's recommendation for HMAC-SHA1 and exactly what apps/api/src/totp.ts's generateSecret() issues. The service refuses a shorter secret.

totp.why: RFC 6238 through the identity service's own implementation, imported rather than written again: one TOTP in this repository, checked against the RFC's vectors in one place. The three numbers are that module's DIGITS, STEP_SECONDS and DRIFT_STEPS, repeated here only because the screen cannot import a module that needs node:crypto — scripts/check-boundaries.mjs fails the build when they disagree. Every accepted code is burned: the step it came from, and every step before it, is refused afterwards.

session.why: A random 256-bit id, held in the service's memory only — a restart signs the founder out, and nothing about a session is ever written down. Two hours from sign-in and not a second more — fifteen minutes until the founder's amendment of 28 September 2026, when the same sign-in came to unlock the Control Tower's settings for a working session — and there is no renewal, because a session that renews itself is one that outlives the person who opened it. One session at a time: a new sign-in ends the previous one. The __Host- prefix makes the browser refuse the cookie unless it is Secure, has Path=/ and names no Domain, so no other name under mythuso.co.za can set or read it; HttpOnly keeps it from every script, SameSite=Strict from every other site's page.

lockout.why: Five consecutive failures — a wrong password, a wrong or reused code at sign-in, or a wrong or reused code at a reveal — lock founder access for fifteen minutes, for the whole account rather than per address, because there is one account and an attacker has as many addresses as they like. The lock ends every open session. It is refused before any password is hashed, so it is also what keeps a stranger from spending the box's memory on scrypt. The price is that a stranger can keep the founder locked out: that is the residual risk docs/governance/FOUNDER-ACCESS.md records, and it is the right way round.

gate._note: Since 28 September 2026 the founder's session also unlocks the settings editors in the Control Tower. The gate lives in the browser (apps/web/src/lib/founder-gate.ts): it asks the same session state the reveal panel does, and opens the editor only when the service says the founder is signed in. Where the service says founder access is dark, or does not answer at all — a local preview, a test — the editor is open as a preview, because every setting in the web preview lives in the tab's memory and reaches no patient; the screen says so in previewSentence. This is a gate on a preview until the service keeps a settings history, at which point the settings routes take the session cookie and the browser's gate stops being the only one.

words.lockedHeading: Sign in to change a setting
words.lockedSentence: Founder access is switched on for this server, so a setting is changed only by the founder, signed in with the password and an authenticator code. One sign-in lasts {minutes} minutes and unlocks every settings editor in the Control Tower.
words.checkingSentence: Asking the assistant service whether the founder is signed in…
words.openSentence: Signed in as the founder. Settings can be changed on this screen until the session ends, {minutes} minutes after sign-in.
words.previewSentence: Founder access is not switched on here, so these settings are a preview: a change lives in this tab's memory, reaches no patient, and a reload puts the defaults back.

door._note: The Control Tower's door, on the founder's instruction of 28 September 2026. In production, opening the Control Tower or the back office — /app/?role=control-tower, /app/?role=back-office, or either role's button on the demo login — draws the founder's two-factor sign-in first, and the portal only while the assistant service says the founder's session is live: the same password and authenticator code, the same four routes, the same cookie, lock and burned codes as the reveal panel above, and the reveal panel's own form (apps/web/src/shells/FounderGate.tsx draws it through a dynamic import, so there is one sign-in form in the product). It fails closed: where the service says founder access is dark, or does not answer at all, the door stays shut and says so in the contract's own sentence, and never falls through to the portal. Sign-out puts the door back. Outside production it is drawn only when the address carries the parameter below, which is how the journeys in tests/founder-gate.spec.ts cover it and how every other Control Tower journey stays exactly as it was; the demo login's buttons open the same door the address does, and that is proved against the built app rather than by carrying the parameter through the role switcher, which is on the patient's first load.

decision.what: When you click on Control Tower it must bring logins with 2FA.

door.why: This door admits one person, the founder, and it is not an admin login system. The fifteen administration layers behind gate G16 — accounts, roles, permissions, tenants, a record of who changed what — still do not exist, and a door drawn to look like their sign-in would be the overstated readiness this codebase refuses everywhere else; so the door says in its own sentence that no other account exists yet. The patient, nurse, doctor and partner previews are not behind it: they are demonstrations on synthetic data, with nothing to protect and nothing to grant, and the demo login still says so on every one of them. The parameter is the developer's and the journey's way to draw the door where import.meta.env.PROD is false; it grants nothing, because the door itself grants nothing — every factor is checked by the service, and the door only asks it and draws the answer. What the door decides is drawn, never what is allowed.

words.heading: The founder's door
words.sentence: The Control Tower opens to the founder alone, signed in with the password and an authenticator code. No other account exists yet: this is one person's door, not a sign-in for administrators.
words.holding: Nothing of the Control Tower is drawn until the founder is signed in.

request.why: Every founder route refuses a request that does not carry the custom header, or whose Sec-Fetch-Site is present and anything but same-origin. A page on another site cannot send the header without a CORS preflight, and the service's origin policy grants no such header to anybody (lib/origin-policy.ts allows content-type alone), so a cross-site form or fetch is refused before a password is read. The cookie's SameSite=Strict is the second lock on the same door.

reveal.why: Exactly two names, and a name outside them is refused before the environment is read: never the password hash, never the TOTP secret, never an endpoint, never anything a future line in an env file might hold. The fingerprint is the first sixteen hex characters of the key's SHA-256 — the same sixteen configure-assistant-env.sh prints and the register records — so the founder can compare without revealing. A revealed key lives in one React component's state and is wiped after thirty seconds, on sign-out, when the tab is hidden and when the screen is left.

audit.why: One line per sign-in attempt, sign-out, metadata read and reveal, each carrying the event, the outcome, and — for a reveal — the key's name and fingerprint prefix. Never a password, a code, a cookie or a value: the line is built by one function whose parameters cannot carry any of them. Since 28 September 2026 the same function writes one line per settings read and change (carrying the setting's key), and per provider read, key set, key deletion, enable change, test and log read (carrying the card and, for a key set, the new key's fingerprint prefix) — and every line of an accepted sign-in or of an act inside a session is also appended to the audit file in the service's state directory, which is what GET /v1/founder/providers/{card}/logs reads back. Since 1 October 2026 a refusal met before any session exists — cross-site, dark, no live session, a refused sign-in — goes to the journal alone: the file is never trimmed and sits on a disk five other sites share, and a stranger's knocking had been both growing it and pushing the founder's own lines out of a card's tail. The logs route reads only the file's last logsReadBytes, so what it costs is bounded by that window and not by how long the service has run.

ownership.what: I need to be able to control all these aspects, I am the owner.
ownership.why: Two facts made the Control Tower's settings and provider controls a preview: a setting saved there lived only in the browser tab while the speak route read the contract's defaults, so a founder who made every presentation voice male still heard a female voice on the test; and a provider key could be set only over SSH, so every registry action was disabled for want of a vault. Both are now the assistant service's, behind the same founder session: an append-only settings history the speak route reads, each change recorded against the founder's session (recorded, not cryptographically signed: whoever can write the state directory can write the file), and a key vault whose values never leave the box. Where the service has no state directory or no vault key, each refuses and says so; nothing here changes what a clinical-delivery register is read with.

state.why: The service kept nothing on disk until 28 September 2026, and it still keeps nothing a patient said: the state directory holds the founder's settings history, the encrypted vault, the founder audit and, since 1 October 2026, the month's count of characters the cloud voice has read (speech-ceiling.json, so the administrator's monthly ceiling survives a restart), and nothing else. deploy/ops/assistant-api.service declares it as a systemd StateDirectory and hands its path to the process in this variable; a process started without the variable — a developer's shell, a test — reads the contract's defaults, answers every founder read, and refuses every founder write with founder-state-unavailable rather than keeping a change it would lose at the next restart. Every file is written 0600, appended to or replaced atomically, and never edited.

settings.why: The founder's changes are held to the same shared rules the web preview and every engine's settings route use — proposeChange() over the assistant block, so a refused change is refused with the shared sentence — and recorded against the administrator role the block names with the founder as the reference, because the founder is the only administrator today. The history is a JSON-lines file: one accepted change per line, in the shared Change shape, replayed at start-up over the contract's defaults, and a file with a gap or a repeat stops the service starting rather than being read around. The speak route reads the presentation voice and the speech settings in force from it; a clinical-delivery register still reads the platform default whatever the history says.
settings.readIsFounderGated: GET /v1/founder/settings carries no secret, and it is still the founder's: the history names who changed how the assistant speaks and why, and the founder's session is the only authentication this service has — an unauthenticated read would be readable by anybody on the internet, and the Control Tower's own reads already are. The web reads what is in force through it when signed in and falls back to the contract's defaults when it is not.

keyShape.why: A provider key is printable ASCII with no space in it, at least sixteen characters and at most five hundred and twelve. The key stored on 22 September 2026 was 140 characters with spaces in it — text pasted in beside it — and the health route said the voice was configured while every request failed; a value that cannot be a key is refused at the door with founder-key-malformed.

vault.why: vault.json in the state directory holds each provider key encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a master key the founder's env file carries — thirty-two random bytes, base64, written once by configure-founder-access.sh and never printed — so root reads ciphertext in one file and the key in another, and a backup of the state directory alone reveals nothing. The cards are exactly the built providers whose card in packages/catalog/api-registry.json names a key variable; the two Alibaba cards share one DashScope key, so setting it on either configures both. Every adapter and configured() read a credential through one function whose precedence is the vault's value, then the environment, then not configured; a card the founder has disabled answers not configured for every variable of its card, so a disabled provider is never called — the registry's own refusal. The reveal route's allowlist is unchanged and the vault never reveals: what the founder reads back is the last four characters, the SHA-256 fingerprint prefix (the same length the reveal shows), when and by whom, and never a value. Setting or deleting a key and changing whether a provider is enabled each ask for a fresh authenticator code on top of the session, as a reveal does; reading metadata, testing a provider and reading its logs do not. A test is one cheap authenticated call to the provider's own listing — voices, models, the account — never a patient's words, and answers ok, refused, unreachable or failed with the latency, never the key. The residency rule is unchanged: an offshore speech provider with a key in the vault is still refused for health-information routes in production while docs/governance/DATA-RESIDENCY-OPTIONS.md §7 is blank.

words.heading: Founder access
words.intro: The founder may sign in here and reveal the two Azure keys the assistant service holds, one at a time, with a fresh authenticator code for each. Nobody else can, and nothing on this panel is stored in the browser.
words.checking: Asking the assistant service whether founder access is switched on…
words.notAnswered: The assistant service did not answer, so founder access cannot be reached from here.
words.codeHint: The code your authenticator app shows now. Each code works once.
words.signedIn: Signed in as the founder. The session ends by itself {minutes} minutes after sign-in.
words.revealCodeHint: A code you have not used yet — wait for your app to show the next one if you have just signed in.
words.copied: Copied. Clear your clipboard when you are done with it.
words.copyFailed: The browser would not copy it.
words.wipes: This key is wiped from the screen after {seconds} seconds, when you sign out, when you leave this screen and when the tab is hidden.
words.wiped: The key was wiped from the screen.
words.settingsHeading: Settings in force on the server
words.settingsSaved: Saved to the server. The next spoken answer of that register reads it.
words.settingsNotPersisted: This server has no state directory, so a change cannot be kept: it would be lost at the next restart, and the service refuses it rather than pretend.
words.vaultIntro: A key typed here is sent once to the assistant service, encrypted on the server, and never shown again — not to you, not to anybody. What you read back is its last four characters and a fingerprint.
words.vaultLocked: The server has no vault key, so a provider key cannot be stored. Run configure-founder-access.sh on the box, then restart the service.
words.keyHint: Paste the key exactly as the provider shows it, with nothing around it. It is checked for shape, stored encrypted, and never shown again.
words.disabled: Switched off: nothing in MyThuso calls this provider until it is switched on again.
words.testRefused: The provider refused the key ({status}). Check it in the provider's own console.
words.testUnreachable: The provider did not answer within {seconds} seconds.
words.testFailed: The provider answered with an error ({status}).
words.fromEnvironment: Set in the server's environment file, not in the vault. Storing a key here takes precedence over it.
words.noLogs: Nothing recorded for this provider yet.
